$schema-note: WIN-260 (M2.5). Every guard this dimension added, and the exact edit that must break it. Same shape as the per-adapter `mutations-*.json` ledgers under packages/adapters/*: `from` is the committed text, `to` is the mutant, `suites` are the files that must be run, and `kills` names the CASE that has to fail. An entry whose mutant leaves every suite green is a guard that is not a guard.
purpose: ONE file rather than five, and that is the departure from the per-package convention. WIN-260's guards span three adapter directories (redis-cache, postgres-tenancy, outbox), two contexts (jobs, memory), the kernel and a gate script, because the dimension is a cross-cutting one: a request identifier that reaches the store, a code that maps to a status, and a reservation that survives a race. A sweep split five ways could not be re-run as one thing, and the whole value of a ledger is that somebody else can re-run it.
procedure: For each entry: apply `to` in place of `from`, run `pnpm build:v1` (cross-package imports resolve through dist, so a mutation in a context is invisible to an adapter suite until the solution is rebuilt), run every file in `suites`, and record which named case failed. Revert. The container suites run ON THE MAC MINI under colima; nothing here starts a daemon on a laptop. A mutant the COMPILER refuses is not a kill for this purpose: it proves the types hold, not that a suite catches a behaviour change, so three entries were rewritten into mutants that compile. Recorded result on the Mac mini at 25568a20 (and the three rewrites re-run separately): 15 entries, 15 killed by a named case, 0 declared unfalsifiable.

mutations.name: M-260-01 reserve: the claim loses its NX
mutations.note: The whole reserve-once property, deleted by two characters. It still compiles, and it still passes every in-memory test in the tree — which is why `client.ts` names the command by intent rather than by spelling, and why the racing suite exists.
kills: two identical requests racing: exactly ONE reserves, and the loser sees the winner
EIGHT identical requests racing: exactly ONE reserves
the racing losers all replay the SAME result, and the work ran ONCE

mutations.name: M-260-02 settle: XX becomes an unconditional write
mutations.from: const written = await connection.overwrite(reservationKey(key), encode(reservation), ttlSeconds);
mutations.to:
await connection.write(reservationKey(key), encode(reservation), ttlSeconds);
        const written = true;
mutations.note: A settle that recreates an expired key lets a request replay long after its window closed. Only a real server can refute this: the key has to actually expire.
kills: settle does NOT resurrect a reservation the server has already expired

mutations.name: M-260-03 reserve: the loser is told nothing was there
mutations.note: The port's reason for carrying the incumbent at all: without it the loser of a race has to re-run the job to find out what happened.
kills: two identical requests racing: exactly ONE reserves, and the loser sees the winner
a completed reservation replays its result to a later, separate connection
reads the incumbent when it LOSES, and reports it as readable

mutations.name: M-260-04 the keyspace loses the environment
mutations.note: One tenant's retry replaying another tenant's result is the worst outcome this port can produce, and it is one interpolation away.
kills: two environments do not collide on one request id
puts the environment IN the key, so two environments cannot collide

mutations.name: M-260-05 a read failure is reported as an absent record
mutations.note: `absent` is a positive answer from a working store; an unreadable incumbent is no answer at all. Merging them tells a caller a conflict nobody established.
kills: FAILS CLOSED when the claim is refused and the incumbent cannot be read

mutations.name: M-260-06 the unpromised-code guard is removed
mutations.from:
if (!isJobExecutionErrorCode(code)) return unreadableRecord("unpromised-code");
      return readableRecord(failedReservation(branded, code));
mutations.note: The READ side of the promise `execute-job.ts::settle` makes on the write side. Settle refuses to CACHE an unpromised code; without this, a record written by a peer on another contract version is replayed onto the wire under a contract that says the set is closed. The mutant CASTS rather than deletes, because deleting the guard alone does not compile — and a mutant the compiler refuses proves the types work, not that the suites do.
kills: REFUSES a cached failure whose code this major never promised
reports UNPROMISED-CODE for a cached failure this major never promised
a record whose failure code this major never promised is REFUSED, not replayed

mutations.name: M-260-07 the four replay refusals collapse back into one code
mutations.note: The defect this issue was pointed at, reinstated exactly. It is the state the branch inherited: four facts, one IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT, indistinguishable in a log and to a caller.
kills: gives each unreadable reason its OWN code, distinct from a real conflict
tells the three unreadable reservations apart, and apart from a real CONFLICT
E6 — two identical raises in one function are refused unless registered

mutations.name: M-260-08 the cache TTL guard is removed
mutations.note: The port's second property. Without the guard the refusal arrives from the driver as MEMORY_CACHE_UNAVAILABLE — a caller defect reported as an outage, which a caller would retry forever.
kills: REFUSES a non-positive or fractional TTL before any command is sent

mutations.name: M-260-09 the blank-namespace guard is removed
mutations.note: The port says a blank prefix "would be a flush of the whole keyspace". With the guard gone the pattern becomes `*` and the sweep clears every other owner's namespace on a shared server.
kills: REFUSES a blank prefix before any command is sent

mutations.name: M-260-10 the namespace glob is no longer escaped
mutations.note: A namespace containing `*` or `[` would then match more keys than it names, in the one bulk destructive operation in this directory.
kills: escapes glob metacharacters, so a prefix names only itself

mutations.name: M-260-11 the transaction stops stamping the request identifier
mutations.note: The state the branch inherited: a request identifier minted at the process edge that reaches nothing. The mutant deletes the whole stamp rather than nulling the reference, because the narrowed `null` does not compile and a compiler refusal is not a suite catching a behaviour change. Only PostgreSQL can refute this one: the assertion is what the SERVER reports.
kills: POSTGRESQL reports the identifier the edge decided on, inside the transaction
the option PostgreSQL answers for is the one the exported constant names
a row written under a correlation is DURABLE, and the setting is not

mutations.name: M-260-12 the setting becomes session-scoped instead of transaction-local
mutations.note: The reason this is not `application_name`. A per-session value stays attached to a pooled connection, so the NEXT request to borrow it is labelled with the previous request's identifier — worse than no label, because it is wrong rather than missing.
kills: the identifier is TRANSACTION-local, so it cannot leak onto the next request

mutations.name: M-260-13 the outbox stops stamping a draft that named no request
mutations.note: Every one of the eight drafts the tree appends supplies `requestId: null`, so without the stamp the envelope's correlation field is populated by nothing, ever. The mutant returns the draft untouched — the state before this issue — rather than nulling the reference, which does not compile.
kills: stamps the request in flight onto a draft that named none
the stamped id survives the drain, so a consumer inherits it

mutations.name: M-260-14 the outbox overwrites a request the producer named
mutations.from:
if (draft.requestId !== null) return draft;
    const reference = correlation?.current() ?? null;
mutations.note: An event appended while replaying work on behalf of an EARLIER request belongs to that request. An overwrite relabels history with whatever happens to be in flight.
kills: does NOT overwrite a request the producer named

mutations.name: M-260-15 the taxonomy stops refusing a code with no mapping
mutations.note: E9 and E1 are the two halves of "a gate that refuses an error code with no mapping". This removes E1; a code minted in any of the seventeen contexts then reaches the wire with no status behind it, and the gate says ok.
kills: E1 — a minted code with no taxonomy entry is refused
the rule list and the fixture agree on which rules exist
